This is a slightly updated version of lectures notes for a course on analytic geometry taught in the winter term 2019/20 at the University of Bonn. The material presented is part of joint work with Dustin Clausen. This is intended as a stable citable version of the material. In the first half of this course, we develop the basic theory of liquid real vector spaces, which we used in another course to give a new approach to complex-analytic geometry. In the second half, we gave a tentative definition of a category of analytic spaces that contains (for example) adic spaces and complex-analytic spaces. While the precise definition of analytic spaces represents an abandoned stepping stone on our way to define analytic stacks and hence should be seen as a historical artifact, much of the surrounding discussion stays very relevant.

Lectures on Analytic Geometry Preface This is a slightly updated version of lectures notes for a course on analytic geometry taught in the winter term 2019/20 at the University of Bonn. The material presented is part of joint work with Dustin Clausen. This is intended as a stable citable version of the material. In the first half of this course, we develop the basic theory of liquid real vector spaces, which is used in [ CS22 ] to give a new approach to complex-analytic geometry. In the second half, we gave a tentative definition of a category of analytic spaces that contains (for example) adic spaces and complex-analytic spaces. While the precise definition of analytic spaces represents an abandoned stepping stone on our way to define analytic stacks in [ CS26 ] and hence should be seen as a historical artifact, much of the surrounding discussion stays very relevant. May 2026, Peter Scholze 0.1. Lecture I: Introduction Mumford writes in Curves and their Jacobians : “[Algebraic geometry] seems to have acquired the reputation of being esoteric, exclusive, and very abstract, with adherents who are secretly plotting to take over all the rest of mathematics. In one respect this last point is accurate.” For some reason, this secret plot has so far stopped short of taking over analysis. The goal of this course is to launch a new attack, turning functional analysis into a branch of commutative algebra, and various types of analytic geometry (like manifolds) into algebraic geometry. Whether this will make these subjects equally esoteric will be left to the reader’s judgement. What do we mean by analytic geometry? We mean a version of algebraic geometry that (1) instead of merely allowing polynomial rings as its basic building blocks, allows rings of convergent power series as basic building blocks; (2) instead of being able to define open subsets only by the nonvanishing of functions, one can define open subsets by asking that a function is small, say less than 1 1 ; (3) strictly generalizes algebraic geometry in the sense that the category of schemes, the theory of quasicoherent sheaves over them, etc., all embed fully faithfully into the corresponding analytic category. The author always had the impression that the highly categorical techniques of algebraic geometry could not possibly be applied in analytic situations; and certainly not over the real numbers. 1 1 1 In the nonarchimedean case, the theory of adic spaces goes a long way towards fulfilling these goals, but it has its shortcomings: Notably, it lacks a theory of quasicoherent sheaves, and in the nonnoetherian case the general formalism does not work well (e.g. the structure presheaf fails to be sheaf). Moreover, the language of adic spaces cannot easily be modified to cover complex manifolds. This is possible by using Berkovich spaces, but again there is no theory of quasicoherent sheaves etc. The goal of this course is to correct this impression. How can one build algebraic geometry? One perspective is that one starts with the abelian category Ab \mathrm{Ab} of abelian groups, with its symmetric monoidal tensor product. Then one can consider rings R R in this category (which are just usual rings), and over any ring R R one can consider modules M M in that category (which are just usual R R -modules). Now to any R R , one associates the space Spec ⁡ R \Spec R , essentially by declaring that (basic) open subsets of Spec ⁡ R \Spec R correspond to localizations R ⁡ [ f − 1 ] R[f^{-1}] of R R . One can then glue these Spec ⁡ R \Spec R ’s together along open subsets to form schemes, and accordingly the category of R R -modules glues to form the category of quasicoherent sheaves. Now how to build analytic geometry? We are basically stuck with the first step: We want an abelian category of some kind of topological abelian groups (together with a symmetric monoidal tensor product that behaves reasonably). Unfortunately, topological abelian groups do not form an abelian category: A map of topological abelian groups that is an isomorphism of underlying abelian groups but merely changes the topology, say ( ℝ , discrete ​ topology ) → ( ℝ , natural ​ topology ) , (\mathbb{R},\mathrm{discrete\ topology})\to(\mathbb{R},\mathrm{natural\ topology}), has trivial kernel and cokernel, but is not an isomorphism. This problem was solved in the course on condensed mathematics last semester, [ Sch19 ] , by replacing the category of topological spaces with the much more algebraic category of condensed sets, and accordingly topological abelian groups with abelian group objects in condensed sets, i.e. condensed abelian groups. Let us recall the definition. Definition 0.1.1 . Consider the pro-étale site ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} of the point ∗ \ast , i.e. the category ProFin ≅ Pro ⁡ ( Fin ) \ProFin\cong\Pro(\Fin) of profinite sets S S with covers given by finite families of jointly surjective maps. A condensed set is a sheaf on ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} ; similarly, a condensed abelian group, ring, etc. is a sheaf of abelian groups, rings, etc. on ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} . 2 2 2 As discussed last semester, this definition has minor set-theoretic issues. We explained then how to resolve them; we will mostly ignore the issues in these lectures. As for sheaves on any site, it is then true that a condensed abelian group, ring, etc. is the same as an abelian group object/ring object/etc. in the category of condensed sets: for example, a condensed abelian group is a condensed set M M together with a map M × M → M M\times M\to M (the addition map) of condensed sets making certain diagrams commute that codify commutativity and associativity, and admits an inverse map. More concretely, a condensed set is a functor X : ProFin op → Sets X:\ProFin^{\mathrm{op}}\to\Sets such that (1) one has X ( ∅ ) = ∗ X(\emptyset)=\ast , and for all profinite sets S 1 S_{1} , S 2 S_{2} , the map X ⁡ ( S 1 ⊔ S 2 ) → X ⁡ ( S 1 ) × X ⁡ ( S 2 ) X(S_{1}\sqcup S_{2})\to X(S_{1})\times X(S_{2}) is bijective; (2) for any surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S of profinite sets, the map X ⁡ ( S ) → { x ∈ X ⁡ ( S ′ ) ∣ p 1 ∗ ​ ( x ) = p 2 ∗ ​ ( x ) ∈ X ⁡ ( S ′ × S S ′ ) } X(S)\to\{x\in X(S^{\prime})\mid p_{1}^{\ast}(x)=p_{2}^{\ast}(x)\in X(S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime})\} is bijective, where p 1 , p 2 : S ′ × S S ′ → S ′ p_{1},p_{2}:S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime}\to S^{\prime} are the two projections. How to think about a condensed set? The value X ⁡ ( ∗ ) X(\ast) should be thought of as the underlying set, and intuitively X ⁡ ( S ) X(S) is the space of continuous maps from S S into X X . For example, if T T is a topological space, one can define a condensed X = T ¯ X=\underline{T} via T ¯ ​ ( S ) = Cont ⁡ ( S , T ) , \underline{T}(S)=\Cont(S,T), the set of continuous maps from S S into T T . One can verify that this defines a condensed set. 3 3 3 There are some set-theoretic subtleties with this assertion if T T does not satisfy the separation axiom T ​ 1 T1 , i.e. its points are not closed; we will only apply this functor under this assumption. Part (1) is clear, and for part (2) the key point is that any surjective map of profinite sets is a quotient map. For example, in analysis a central notion is that of a sequence x 0 , x 1 , … x_{0},x_{1},\ldots converging to x ∞ x_{\infty} . This is codified by maps from the profinite set S = { 0 , 1 , … , ∞ } S=\{0,1,\ldots,\infty\} (the one-point compactification ℕ ∪ { ∞ } \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} of ℕ \mathbb{N} ) into X X . Allowing more general profinite sets makes it possible to capture more subtle convergence behaviour. For example, if T T is a compact Hausdorff space and you have any sequence of points x 0 , x 1 , … ∈ T x_{0},x_{1},\ldots\in T , then it is not necessarily the case that it converges in T T ; but one can always find convergent subsequences. More precisely, for each ultrafilter 𝒰 \mathcal{U} on ℕ \mathbb{N} , one can take the limit along the ultrafilter. In fact, this gives a map β ​ ℕ → T \beta\mathbb{N}\to T from the space β ​ ℕ \beta\mathbb{N} of ultrafilters on ℕ \mathbb{N} . The space β ​ ℕ \beta\mathbb{N} is a profinite set, known as the Stone–Čech compactification of ℕ \mathbb{N} ; it is the initial compact Hausdorff space to which ℕ \mathbb{N} maps (by an argument along these lines). We have the following result about the relation between topological spaces and condensed sets, proved last semester except for the last assertion in part (4), which can be found for example in [ BS15 , Lemma 4.3.7] . 4 4 4 Again, some of these assertions run into minor set-theoretic problems; we refer to the notes from last semester. Importantly, everything is valid on the nose when restricted to topological spaces with closed points, and quasiseparated condensed sets; in particular, points (3) and (4) are true as stated. Proposition 0.1.2 . Consider the functor T ↦ T ¯ T\mapsto\underline{T} from topological spaces to condensed sets. (1) The functor has a left adjoint X ↦ X ​ ( ∗ ) top X\mapsto X(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}} sending any condensed set X X to its underlying set X ⁡ ( ∗ ) X(\ast) equipped with the quotient topology arising from the map ⨆ S , a ∈ X ⁡ ( S ) S → X ⁡ ( ∗ ) . \bigsqcup_{S,a\in X(S)}S\to X(\ast). (2) Restricted to compactly generated (e.g., first-countable, e.g., metrizable) topological spaces, the functor is fully faithful. (3) The functor induces an equivalence between the category of compact Hausdorff spaces, and quasicompact quasiseparated condensed sets. (4) The functor induces a fully faithful functor from the category of compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces (the standard “convenient category of topological spaces” in algebraic topology), to quasiseparated condensed sets. The category of quasiseparated condensed sets is equivalent to the category of ind-compact Hausdorff spaces ` ​ ` ​ lim → i ⁡ " ​ T i ``\varinjlim_{i}"T_{i} where all transition maps T i → T j T_{i}\to T_{j} are closed immersions. If X 0 ↪ X 1 ↪ … X_{0}\hookrightarrow X_{1}\hookrightarrow\ldots is a sequence of compact Hausdorff spaces with closed immersions and X = lim → n ⁡ X n X=\varinjlim_{n}X_{n} as a topological space, the map lim → n ⁡ X n ¯ → X ¯ \varinjlim_{n}\underline{X_{n}}\to\underline{X} is an isomorphism of condensed sets. In particular, lim → n ⁡ X n ¯ \varinjlim_{n}\underline{X_{n}} comes from a topological space. Here the notions of quasicompactness/quasiseparatedness are general notions applying to sheaves on any (coherent) site. In our case, a condensed set X X is quasicompact if there is some profinite S S with a surjective map S → X S\to X . A condensed set X X is quasiseparated if for any two profinite sets S 1 , S 2 S_{1},S_{2} with maps to X X , the fibre product S 1 × X S 2 S_{1}\times_{X}S_{2} is quasicompact. The functor in (4) is close to an equivalence, and in any case (4) asserts that quasiseparated condensed sets can be described in very classical terms. Let us also mention the following related result. Lemma 0.1.3 . Let X 0 ↪ X 1 ↪ … X_{0}\hookrightarrow X_{1}\hookrightarrow\ldots and Y 0 ↪ Y 1 ↪ … Y_{0}\hookrightarrow Y_{1}\hookrightarrow\ldots be two sequences of compact Hausdorff spaces with closed immersions. Then, inside the category of topological spaces, the natural map ⋃ n X n × Y n → ( ⋃ n X n ) × ( ⋃ n Y n ) \bigcup_{n}X_{n}\times Y_{n}\to(\bigcup_{n}X_{n})\times(\bigcup_{n}Y_{n}) is a homeomorphism; i.e. the product on the right is equipped with its compactly generated topology. Proof. The map is clearly a continuous bijection. In general, for a union like ⋃ n X n \bigcup_{n}X_{n} , open subsets U U are the subsets of the form ⋃ n U n \bigcup_{n}U_{n} where each U n ⊂ X n U_{n}\subset X_{n} is open. Thus, let U ⊂ ⋃ n X n × Y n U\subset\bigcup_{n}X_{n}\times Y_{n} be any open subset, written as a union of open subset U n ⊂ X n × Y n U_{n}\subset X_{n}\times Y_{n} , and pick any point ( x , y ) ∈ U (x,y)\in U . Then for any large enough n n (so that ( x , y ) ∈ X n × Y n (x,y)\in X_{n}\times Y_{n} ), we can find open neighborhoods V n ⊂ X n V_{n}\subset X_{n} of x x in X n X_{n} and W n ⊂ Y n W_{n}\subset Y_{n} of y y in Y n Y_{n} , such that V n × W n ⊂ U n V_{n}\times W_{n}\subset U_{n} . In fact, we can ensure that even V ¯ n × W ¯ n ⊂ U n \overline{V}_{n}\times\overline{W}_{n}\subset U_{n} by shrinking V n V_{n} and W n W_{n} . Constructing the V n V_{n} and W n W_{n} inductively, we may then moreover ensure V ¯ n ⊂ V n + 1 \overline{V}_{n}\subset V_{n+1} and W ¯ n ⊂ W n + 1 \overline{W}_{n}\subset W_{n+1} . Then V = ⋃ n V n ⊂ ⋃ n X n V=\bigcup_{n}V_{n}\subset\bigcup_{n}X_{n} and W = ⋃ n W n ⊂ ⋃ n Y n W=\bigcup_{n}W_{n}\subset\bigcup_{n}Y_{n} are open, and V × W = ⋃ n V n × W n ⊂ U V\times W=\bigcup_{n}V_{n}\times W_{n}\subset U contains ( x , y ) (x,y) , showing that U U is open in the product topology. ∎ We asserted above that one should think of X ⁡ ( ∗ ) X(\ast) as the underlying set of X X , and about X ⁡ ( S ) X(S) as the continous maps from S S into X X . Note however that in general the map X ⁡ ( S ) → ∏ s ∈ S X ⁡ ( { s } ) = ∏ s ∈ S X ⁡ ( ∗ ) = Map ⁡ ( S , X ⁡ ( ∗ ) ) X(S)\to\prod_{s\in S}X(\{s\})=\prod_{s\in S}X(\ast)=\mathrm{Map}(S,X(\ast)) may not be injective, and in fact it may and does happen that X ( ∗ ) = ∗ X(\ast)=\ast but X ( S ) ≠ ∗ X(S)\neq\ast for large S S . However, for quasiseparated condensed sets, this map is always injective (as follows from (4) above), and in particular a quasiseparated condensed set X X is trivial as soon as X ⁡ ( ∗ ) X(\ast) is trivial. The critical property of condensed sets is however exactly that they can also handle non-Hausdorff situations (i.e., non-quasiseparated situations in the present technical jargon) well. For example, condensed abelian groups, like sheaves of abelian groups on any site, form an abelian category. Considering the example from above and passing to condensed abelian groups, we get a short exact sequence 0 → ( ℝ , discrete ​ topology ) ¯ → ( ℝ , natural ​ topology ) ¯ → Q → 0 0\to\underline{(\mathbb{R},\mathrm{discrete\ topology})}\to\underline{(\mathbb{R},\mathrm{natural\ topology})}\to Q\to 0 of condensed abelian groups, for a condensed abelian group Q Q satisfying Q ( S ) = Cont ( S , ℝ ) / { locally constant maps S → ℝ } Q(S)=\Cont(S,\mathbb{R})/\{\mathrm{locally\ constant\ maps\ }S\to\mathbb{R}\} for any profinite set S S . 5 5 5 It is nontrivial that this formula for Q Q is correct: A priori, this describes the quotient on the level of presheaves, and one might have to sheafify. However, using H 1 ​ ( S , M ) = 0 H^{1}(S,M)=0 for any profinite set S S and discrete abelian group M M , as proved last semester, one gets the result by using the long exact cohomology sequence. In particular Q ⁡ ( ∗ ) = 0 Q(\ast)=0 while Q ⁡ ( S ) ≠ 0 Q(S)\neq 0 for general S S : There are plenty of non-locally constant maps S → ℝ S\to\mathbb{R} for profinite sets S S , say any convergent sequence that is not eventually constant. In particular, Q Q is not quasiseparated. We see that enlarging topological abelian groups into an abelian category precisely forces us to include non-quasiseparated objects, in such a way that a quotient M 1 / M 2 M_{1}/M_{2} still essentially remembers the topology on both M 1 M_{1} and M 2 M_{2} . At this point, we have our desired abelian category, the category Cond ⁡ ( Ab ) \Cond(\Ab) of condensed abelian groups. Again, like for sheaves of abelian groups on any site, it has a symmetric monoidal tensor product (representing bilinear maps in the obvious way). We could then follow the same steps as for schemes. However, the resulting theory does not yet achieve our stated goals: (1) The basic building blocks in algebraic geometry, the polynomial rings, are exactly the free rings on some set I I . As sets are generated by finite sets, really the case of a finite set is relevant, giving rise to the polynomial algebras ℤ ⁡ [ X 1 , … , X n ] \mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] . Similarly, the basic building blocks are now the free rings on a condensed set; as these are generated by profinite sets, one could also just take the free rings on a profinite set S S . But for a profinite set S S , the corresponding free condensed ring generated by S S is not anything like a ring of (convergent) power series. In fact, the underlying ring is simply the free ring on the underlying set of S S , i.e. an infinite polynomial algebra. To further illustrate this point, let us instead consider the free condensed ring A A equipped with an element T ∈ A T\in A with the sequence T , T 2 , … , T n , … T,T^{2},\ldots,T^{n},\ldots converging 0 0 : This is given by A = ℤ ⁡ [ S ] / ( [ ∞ ] = 0 ) A=\mathbb{Z}[S]/([\infty]=0) for the profinite set S = ℕ ∪ { ∞ } S=\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} . The underlying ring of A A is then still the polynomial algebra ℤ ⁡ [ T ] \mathbb{Z}[T] ; it is merely equipped with a nonstandard condensed ring structure. (2) One cannot define open subsets by “putting bounds on functions”. If say over ℚ p \mathbb{Q}_{p} we want to make the locus { | T | ≤ 1 } \{|T|\leq 1\} into an open subset of the affine line, and agree that this closed unit disc should correspond to the algebra of convergent power series ℚ p ​ ⟨ T ⟩ = { ∑ n ≥ 0 a n ​ T n ∣ a n → 0 } \mathbb{Q}_{p}\langle T\rangle=\{\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}T^{n}\mid a_{n}\to 0\} while the affine line corresponds to ℚ p ​ [ T ] \mathbb{Q}_{p}[T] , then being a localization should mean that the multiplication map ℚ p ​ ⟨ T ⟩ ⊗ ℚ p ​ [ T ] ℚ p ​ ⟨ T ⟩ → ℚ p ​ ⟨ T ⟩ \mathbb{Q}_{p}\langle T\rangle\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}[T]}\mathbb{Q}_{p}\langle T\rangle\to\mathbb{Q}_{p}\langle T\rangle should be an isomorphism. However, this is not an isomorphism of condensed abelian groups: On underlying abelian groups, the tensor product is just the usual algebraic tensor product. These failures are not unexpected: We did not yet put in any nontrivial analysis. Somewhere we have to specify which kinds of convergent power series we want to use. Concretely, in a condensed ring R R with a sequence T , T 2 , … , T n , … T,T^{2},\ldots,T^{n},\ldots converging to 0 0 , we want to allow certain power series ∑ n ≥ 0 r n ​ T n \sum_{n\geq 0}r_{n}T^{n} where not almost all of the coefficients r n r_{n} are zero. Hopefully, this specification maintains a nice abelian category that acquires its own tensor product, in such a way that now the tensor product computation in point (2) above works out. Last semester, we developed such a formalism that works very well in nonarchimedean geometry: This is the formalism of solid abelian groups that we will recall in the next lecture. In particular, the solidification of the ring A A considered in (1) is exactly the power series ring ℤ ⁡ [ [ T ] ] \mathbb{Z}[[T]] (with its condensed ring structure coming from the usual topology on the power series ring), and after solidification the tensor product equation in (2) becomes true. Unfortunately, the real numbers ℝ \mathbb{R} are not solid: Concretely, T = 1 2 ∈ ℝ T=\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{R} has the property that its powers go to 0 0 , but not any sum ∑ r n ​ ( 1 2 ) n \sum r_{n}(\frac{1}{2})^{n} with coefficients r n ∈ ℤ r_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} converges in ℝ \mathbb{R} . Thus, the solid formalism breaks down completely over ℝ \mathbb{R} . Now maybe that was expected? After all, the whole formalism is based on the paradigm of resolving nice compact Hausdorff spaces like the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] by profinite sets, and this does not seem like a clever thing to do over the reals; over totally disconnected rings like ℚ p \mathbb{Q}_{p} it of course seems perfectly sensible. However, last semester we promised a theorem on how the formalism might be adapted to cover the reals. The first main goal of this course will be to prove this theorem. 0.2. Lecture II: Solid modules In this lecture, we recall the theory of solid modules that was developed last semester. Recall from the last lecture that we want to put some “completeness” condition on modules in such a way that the free objects behave like some kind of power series. To understand the situation, let us first analyze the structure of free condensed abelian groups. Proposition 0.2.1 . Let S = lim ← i ⁡ S i S=\varprojlim_{i}S_{i} be a profinite set, written as an inverse limit of finite sets S i S_{i} . For any n n , let ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n ⊂ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n}\subset\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] be the subset of formal sums ∑ s ∈ S i n s ​ [ s ] \sum_{s\in S_{i}}n_{s}[s] such that ∑ | n s | ≤ n \sum|n_{s}|\leq n ; this is a finite set, and the natural transition maps ℤ ⁡ [ S j ] → ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \mathbb{Z}[S_{j}]\to\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] preserve these subsets. There is a natural isomorphism of condensed abelian groups ℤ ⁡ [ S ] ≅ ⋃ n lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n ⊂ lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] . \mathbb{Z}[S]\cong\bigcup_{n}\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n}\subset\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]. In particular, ℤ ⁡ [ S ] \mathbb{Z}[S] is a countable union of the profinite sets ℤ ​ [ S ] ≤ n := lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n \mathbb{Z}[S]_{\leq n}:=\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n} . Note that the right-hand side indeed defines a subgroup: The addition on lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] takes ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n × ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n ′ \mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n}\times\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n^{\prime}} into ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n + n ′ \mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n+n^{\prime}} . We also remark that the bound imposed is as an ℓ 1 \ell^{1} -bound, but in fact it is equivalent to an ℓ 0 \ell^{0} -bound, as only finitely many n s n_{s} (in fact, n n of them) can be nonzero. Proof. By definition, ℤ ⁡ [ S ] \mathbb{Z}[S] is the free condensed abelian group on S S , and this is formally given by the sheafification of the functor T ↦ ℤ ⁡ [ Cont ⁡ ( T , S ) ] T\mapsto\mathbb{Z}[\Cont(T,S)] . First, we check that the map ℤ ⁡ [ S ] → lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \mathbb{Z}[S]\to\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] is an injection. First, we observe that the map of underlying abelian groups is injective. This means that given any finite formal sum ∑ j = 1 k n j ​ [ s j ] \sum_{j=1}^{k}n_{j}[s_{j}] where the s j ∈ S s_{j}\in S are distinct elements and n j ≠ 0 n_{j}\neq 0 are integers, one can find some projection S → S i S\to S_{i} such that the image in ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] is nonzero. But we can arrange that the images of the s j s_{j} in S i S_{i} are all distinct, giving the result. Now, assume that f ∈ ℤ ⁡ [ Cont ⁡ ( T , S ) ] f\in\mathbb{Z}[\Cont(T,S)] maps to 0 0 in lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] ​ ( T ) \varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}](T) . In particular, for all t ∈ T t\in T , the specialization f ⁡ ( t ) ∈ ℤ ⁡ [ S ] f(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[S] is zero by the injectivity on underlying abelian groups. We have to see that there is some finite cover of T T by profinite sets T m → T T_{m}\to T such that the preimage of f f in each ℤ ⁡ [ Cont ⁡ ( T m , S ) ] \mathbb{Z}[\Cont(T_{m},S)] is zero. Write f = ∑ j = 1 k n j ​ [ g j ] f=\sum_{j=1}^{k}n_{j}[g_{j}] where g j : T → S g_{j}:T\to S are distinct continuous functions and n j ≠ 0 n_{j}\neq 0 . We argue by induction on k k . For each pair 1 ≤ j < j ′ ≤ k 1\leq j<j^{\prime}\leq k , let T j ​ j ′ ⊂ T T_{jj^{\prime}}\subset T be the closed subset where g j = g j ′ g_{j}=g_{j^{\prime}} . Then the T j ​ j ′ T_{jj^{\prime}} cover T T : Indeed, if t ∈ T t\in T does not lie in any T j ​ j ′ T_{jj^{\prime}} , then all g j ​ ( t ) ∈ S g_{j}(t)\in S are pairwise distinct, and then ∑ j = 1 k n j ​ [ g j ​ ( t ) ] ∈ ℤ ⁡ [ S ] \sum_{j=1}^{k}n_{j}[g_{j}(t)]\in\mathbb{Z}[S] is nontrivial. Thus, we may pass to the cover by the T j ​ j ′ T_{jj^{\prime}} and thereby assume that g j = g j ′ g_{j}=g_{j^{\prime}} for some j ≠ j ′ j\neq j^{\prime} . But this reduces k k , so we win by induction. As observed before, ⋃ n lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n \bigcup_{n}\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n} defines a condensed abelian group, and it admits a map from S = lim ← i ⁡ S i S=\varprojlim_{i}S_{i} ; in particular, as ℤ ⁡ [ S ] \mathbb{Z}[S] is the free condensed abelian group on S S , the map ℤ ⁡ [ S ] → lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ⁡ [ S i ] \mathbb{Z}[S]\to\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}] factors over ⋃ n lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n \bigcup_{n}\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n} . It remains to see that the induced map ℤ ⁡ [ S ] → ⋃ n lim ← i ⁡ ℤ ​ [ S i ] ≤ n \mathbb{Z}[S]\to\bigcup_{n}\varprojlim_{i}\mathbb{Z}[S_{i}]_{\leq n} is surjective.
